text:
Automatic Identification System
Frequently Asked Questions
NOAA Office for Coastal Management
https://marinecadastre.gov/ais
May 2026
AIS Broadcast Points
Do you publish live or near real-time data?
Live data feeds are not available through this platform. The latest available data are hosted on our
website. We do not restrict or embargo any data; data are published as soon as processing is complete.
Do you have data before 2009?
No, 2009 is the earliest year for which data are available.
Do you have AIS for my location?
Data are generally available for the U.S. Exclusive Economic Zone, major inland waterways, the Great
Lakes, and Guam.
Coverage is currently unavailable for remote Pacific territories, foreign waters, or waters extending
more than 40 to 50 miles from the coast. Please see the Alaska-specific note below regarding historical
coverage.
What is your data source?
These data originate from the Nationwide Automatic Identification System (NAIS) operated by the U.S.
Coast Guard. The NAIS comprises approximately 200 land-based receiving stations located near
important navigation routes in the contiguous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and parts of the
Caribbean. This collection also includes data provided by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers for inland
waterways.
1

Do you have AIS data collected by satellite?
No. All data provided here originate from land-based receivers. While some commercial providers
collect and sell satellite AIS data, and some federal agencies purchase these data for specific needs,
those agencies are restricted from distributing satellite data to the public under the terms of their
licensing agreement.
What format is used to publish the data?
• Prior to 2015: Data were published in File Geodatabase format.
• 2015 and onward: All broadcast points are provided in compressed CSV format.
For a year-by-year summary with additional technical details, please refer to the Point Data Summary
table on the AIS home page.
How can I acquire an entire year of data?
To access daily nationwide files from 2015 onward, use the bulk download links on the AIS home page.
For requests under 2 GB, use the AccessAIS application to download data for a custom geographic area
and time period.
Annual products for track and transit counts can be found in the download table on the AIS home page.
These products are derived from original broadcast points and are often easier for casual users to work
with because of their smaller file size and efficient data structure.
Why are data missing for Alaska in certain years?
Broadcast point data are available for Alaska through March 28, 2021. Track and transit count grids do
not exist for this time period, and data gaps are present in the Northern and Arctic regions.
As of March 29, 2021, all Alaska broadcast point data were removed from this collection at the request
of the Marine Exchange of Alaska, which owns most of the regional AIS receiving stations.
Why are some files considerably smaller than the average size?
Vessel traffic volume varies due to natural and human factors, as well as data-collection interruptions
within the NAIS sensor network. Data received from the U.S. Coast Guard typically do not specify the
cause or duration of sensor outages.
We use all records provided by the U.S. Coast Guard and employ quality-control techniques to
document data gaps. Most gaps are brief—lasting from a few hours to a couple of days—and are usually
limited to a small number of receiving stations.
2

Why hasn’t the number of cargo vessels increased over time?
Several factors could influence this trend:
1. Improved reporting accuracy: The U.S. Coast Guard launched educational campaigns to help
vessel owners report their vessel types more accurately.
2. Increased vessel size: The average size of cargo vessels has increased, allowing more cargo to be
moved per ship.
3. Route changes: Some vessels may alter their routes to travel further offshore, outside the range
of the NAIS receivers, to avoid certain emission control areas.
Are accidents or other events removed from the data?
No. Collisions, allisions, and other accidents are preserved in the data. Raw data from the National
Marine Electronics Association (NMEA) are down-sampled to the nearest whole minute. The dataset
comprises all vessels detected by land-based antennas, excluding certain law enforcement and military
vessels exempt for national security reasons. Many smaller vessels are exempt from AIS carriage
requirements due to their length or displacement.
How can I analyze data coverage?
To summarize broadcast point and track data, use an H3 or S2 tessellation to enumerate the magnitude
or presence of data across a grid.
Why do some records appear far from shore, beyond normal radio range?
Signals detected beyond the expected range of land-based antennas often result from the anomalous
propagation of AIS signals (e.g., tropospheric ducting). These data should not be viewed as erroneous or
satellite-derived. Receiving stations at high elevations frequently detect signals from great distances,
especially from commercial vessels with tall infrastructure and high-powered transmitters.
Why are data present over land?
GPS is the primary source for vessel positions. Positional errors can arise from natural, human, or
systematic factors. Furthermore, vessels in narrow inland waterways or those transported by land may
report coordinates that place them on shore.
Are Class B data included?
Yes. Class B data are included, and the class designation is provided for each record after 2017. Class B
data are known to be present in the data starting in 2015, possibly earlier.
Where are the AIS receiver stations located?
The AIS Base Stations dataset and data service can be accessed via the Marine Cadastre Data Registry.
3

Broadcast Point Attributes
Is a data dictionary available?
Yes, a link to the latest data dictionary (2015–2025) is located at the bottom of the AIS web page. Data
for 2009 to 2015 have a different structure and are normalized across three related tables (fig. 1).
Figure 1. Simplified object model for 2009–2015 AIS broadcast points.
Have the vessel type codes been cleaned or modified?
Between 2015 and 2023, the U.S. Coast Guard's Authoritative Vessel Identification Service (AVIS)
database was used to replace specific vessel-dependent values such as vessel_type, length, width, and
draft. The original uncorrected vessel_type code from the raw NMEA record can still be found in the
cargo field for that period.
Beginning in 2024, the AIS Vessel Identification Database (AVID) replaced AVIS. AVID is used primarily to
populate null values or correct gross errors in vessel-dependent fields. For more details on vessel
grouping, refer to NOAA’s AIS Vessel Type and Group Codes (PDF).
4

What is the AIS Vessel Identification Database (AVID)?
AVID is used to verify and enhance vessel identity and characteristics. It integrates 23 sources including
state, federal, and international authorities, as well as the final version of AVIS, into a fuzzy logic model.
This model drives updates for null values and gross errors found in raw NMEA records.
AVID only modifies vessel-dependent values originally input by the mariner. Since its implementation in
January 2024, AVID-based updates have corrected approximately 10–15 percent of records.
How do I interpret the vessel type and cargo codes?
The vessel_type codes are defined in the NMEA specification and documented in the Class A AIS Position
Report (Messages 1,2,3) by the U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center (NAVCEN). The USCG AIS Encoding
Guide (PDF) and NOAA’s AIS Vessel Type and Group Codes (PDF) are helpful resources.
For practical purposes, cargo codes are identical to vessel types. Discrepancies between vessel_type and
cargo typically occur when corrections are imputed to the vessel_type value or the purpose of the
vessel’s voyage changes.
Why would a vessel name change over time?
Vessel names frequently change due to ownership transfers. Because vessel_name is a mariner input
field, it is prone to human error or intentional modification. Sometimes, an AIS transponder (with its
associated Maritime Mobile Service Identity [MMSI]) is transferred to a new owner; at other times, an
owner may retain the transponder for use on an entirely different vessel.
When a name is uncertain or null in the raw NMEA data, the field is updated using the name associated
with that Maritime Mobile Service Identity in AVID. For reliable tracking, use stable identifiers such as
MMSI, IMO, or Call Sign.
Can I group data by vessel type to study trends?
Yes. Similar vessel types from native NMEA data and corrected vessel types can be combined into logical
vessel groups (e.g., combining type 31 and type 1025 into "Towing"). A table of recommended vessel
groups and their corresponding values is available in the Vessel Type and Group Codes (PDF).
Note: The "Other" vessel group contains a wide variety of specific vessel classifications.
What is the difference between vessel-type codes below and above 99?
• 0–99: Standardized NMEA vessel types
• 99–255: Reserved for future use
• Above 999: These are 4-digit AVIS service types. They are not part of the native NMEA stream.
5

From 2015 through 2017, 4-digit AVIS codes were used directly in the correction process. From 2018
through 2023, while AVIS was still used, these codes were mapped to the "best fit" NMEA vessel type
(0–99) during processing.
The vessel type codes in the 1001–1025 range no longer exist. Is there a way to reclassify the 2-digit
vessel type code to the 4-digit pattern?
Not exactly. While the 2-digit and 4-digit codes share similarities and near matches can be made for
most analytical purposes, these codes do not have 1:1 direct mapping.
What does vessel type 59 mean?
According to ITU Resolution 18, type 59 refers to “ships and aircraft of States not Parties to an armed
conflict.”
Technical Guidance
How do I find historical data for a specific vessel?
Download the broadcast point data for your specific geographic and temporal area of interest, then
query the dataset using the mmsi, imo, call_sign, or vessel_name field.
Can I unscramble encrypted MMSI values present in 2009–2014 data?
Yes, a brief user guide and standalone .exe tool for Windows are available in the MMSI Scrambler Tool
ZIP file. Note: Technical support for this script is currently unavailable.
How do I find a vessel owner?
Vessel ownership is not recorded in this AIS dataset. However, the Maritime Mobile Service Identity can
be used to combine this data with other public or licensed maritime databases to retrieve ownership
information.
Are voyage-related data (e.g., Voyage ID, Destination) available?
These values were phased out in 2015 due to inherent inaccuracies. Destination values entered by
mariners are often subjective and inconsistent. Vessel track datasets are available and defined by MMSI,
start/stop times, and distance gaps.
6

How do I interpret Course Over Ground (COG) values?
Course Over Ground values are provided by the vessel’s GPS unit. Errors can occur due to poorly
configured hardware, phase wrapping, or non-north settings.
• Pre-2015 data: If a COG value is negative, calculate a new Course Over Ground using a pair of
latitude and longitude coordinates.
• Sentinel values: A value of 360.0 indicates that COG data are unavailable and should be ignored.
Why do some Speed Over Ground (SOG) values in the pre-2015 data appear incorrect?
Speed Over Ground values are subject to the same GPS-related errors as COG values.
• Pre-2015 data: If a SOG value is negative, calculate a new Speed Over Ground using a pair of
latitude and longitude coordinates.
• Sentinel values: A value of 102.3 indicates that SOG data are not available.
• Outliers: Extreme outliers are occasionally caused by AIS transponders mounted on aircraft
rather than vessels.
Why do the time stamp and local time of an observed vessel differ?
All time stamps in the NMEA record use Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). Local time will differ based
on time zone offsets and daylight saving time adjustments.
How do “Draught” (2009–2014) and “Draft” (2015–Present) compare?
• 2009–2014 (Draught): Reported in decimeters (1/10th of a meter). A value of 255 represents
25.5 meters or greater.
• 2015–Present (Draft): The American spelling was adopted. Units are reported in meters with
1/10-meter resolution.
Be aware that carriage requirements have changed; modern entries typically report the maximum
present static draft.
Are parameters like tonnage, horsepower, or fuel type included?
No, these parameters are not part of the standard AIS broadcast. This information can be obtained from
third-party maritime logistics vendors by using the Maritime Mobile Service Identifier as a relational key.
What does a value of “511” in the heading field represent?
In pre-2015 data, 511 was the default sentinel value that indicated heading data were not available.
7

AIS Track and Transit Counts
What is the cell size of the density grids, and what do the values represent?
The cell size for the 2011/2013 kernel density grids and post-2015 transit count grids is 100 meters.
• Kernel density: These values represent the count of features per unit area, typically visualized as
a heat map.
• Transit counts: These values represent the actual number of unique vessel tracks passing
through a specified cell.
While kernel density analyses generally use point data as an input, the Transit Count product is derived
from the count of unique vessel tracks intersecting a grid cell.
How can I get an estimated time of arrival for a vessel?
Query the end time in the Vessel Track product for the line feature nearest to the destination. For a
more precise estimate, query the base_date_time value for the broadcast point nearest to the
destination.
Why is there a small irregularity in track and transit count data, running north–south in the Gulf of
America?
The track data are constructed on a per ocean basin pattern and then merged into a national dataset.
This process can result in a minor gap or overlaps west of Florida, where the Gulf of America and
Atlantic data subsets meet.
Why are track data absent for Alaska for some years?
Access to broadcast point data for Alaska has been intermittent. Therefore, derived data products, such
as tracks and transit counts, have not been generated.
How do I work with the GeoPackage data format?
First, unzip the compressed file to extract the .gpkg file. The GeoPackage data object is an SQLite
container that holds all the geometry and attribute data. This file can be opened directly by most
modern desktop GIS platforms and accessed via Python libraries.
AccessAIS Provisioning System
What types of AIS data are available from the AccessAIS tool?
AccessAIS is a data provisioning system for broadcast point data. Track and transit count data are not
distributed by this application. However, transit count and other layers are included in the map display
8

to help users orient themselves during the ordering process. New broadcast point data are added to the
tool quarterly; transit count display layers are updated annually.
My order says “Download has expired.” What should I do?
The CSV download link expires after 14 days or once accessed five times, whichever occurs first. If your
link has expired, please submit a new order. Expired orders cannot be recovered or resubmitted.
Why is there a size limit for the download?
Size limits maintain system performance, control costs, and serve the broadest possible audience. For
larger data requests, please use the Bulk Download page.
If records exist back to 2009, why does AccessAIS only host the last five years of data?
Design and cost constraints during tool development determined the maximum storage capacity. That
limit resulted in a five-year rolling order window for available data. Data older than five years remain
available for download from the Bulk Download page.
Does AccessAIS source data originate from a live U.S. Coast Guard feed?
No, these data originate from quarterly historical data requests to the U.S. Coast Guard. The raw data is
then down-sampled and filtered to generate a derived data product for public use. While data from
AccessAIS and the Bulk Download site differ slightly in format and structure, a 2026 upgrade is
scheduled to eliminate these differences.
Are data for inland areas included in AccessAIS?
Yes, data for inland areas are included for locations where the U.S. Coast Guard and the U.S. Army Corps
of Engineers maintain antennas. The presence or absence of data shown in the vessel track or vessel
transit count product is not an absolute indicator of broadcast point data availability. The broadcast
point data are the superset from which vessel track and transit count data are built. In some cases,
broadcast point coverage is sparse, and the track and transit count data products are unpopulated.
Are data available for Alaska?
Coverage in Alaska is inconsistent, both temporally and geographically. Good coverage existed from
2015 to 2017 (especially in northern Alaska), but data are not available after March 29, 2021. Efforts to
backfill these data gaps are ongoing.
Are data available for Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands?
These data are not within AccessAIS at this time. However, broadcast point data for this region can be
acquired via the Bulk Download table and the annual Guam ZIP file folder . Track and transit count data
products for this area were not generated until 2025.
9

How often are new data added to the AccessAIS application?
New broadcast point data are added every 90 days; however, delays may occur due to government
shutdowns or other unforeseen events. The total lag time from data collection to delivery is
approximately 145 to 165 days.
Can I obtain a URL for my area of interest to share with others?
Once your order has been processed, you will receive a shareable URL to download data. The download
can be accessed up to five times within a 14-day window. Download errors can often be resolved by
clearing the browser cache.
Appropriate Use
Can I use these data for regulatory or enforcement purposes?
These data are intended for coastal and ocean planning purposes only.
Can I use and redistribute these data on other websites?
Yes, you may release derived products built from these data. Please cite your data source to promote
transparency.
Who owns the copyright to these data? Can I use it to generate a commercial product?
According to the U.S. Coast Guard Navigation Center:
These data are derived from the U.S. Coast Guard NAIS subject to the conditions of data sharing
category “Level C (Historical Data)” and within the framework of Commandant Instruction
5230.80, Sharing of Information Collected by the Coast Guard Nationwide Automatic
Identification System. The historical data are generally considered public domain.
All provided data may not be used for purposes other than those intended for the disclosure.
Foreign governments, Federal, State, local and tribal government agencies, and non-
governmental entities shall not retransmit or redistribute AIS information (real-time or stored) in
any form other than those intended for the disclosure as approved, and shall not charge a fee for
its usage.
Does NOAA have a terms and condition statement for these data?
As required by 17 U.S.C. § 403, third parties producing copyrighted works consisting
predominantly of the material produced by U.S. government agencies must provide notice with
such work(s) identifying the U.S. Government material incorporated and stating that such
material is not subject to copyright protection within the United States. The information on
10

government web pages is in the public domain and not subject to copyright protection within the
United States unless specifically annotated otherwise (copyright may be held elsewhere). Foreign
copyrights may apply.
Citations and Points of Contact
How do I cite Marine Cadastre data?
NOAA Office for Coastal Management. ([Year]). [Title of Dataset]. Marine Cadastre.
https://marinecadastre.gov.
Who should I list as the point of contact when citing the Marine Cadastre AIS data?
